{"answer": "C3 AND C4 PLANTS UNDER EXTREME HEAT, AND WHICH WILL PRODUCE MORE BIOMASS IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA BY 2045

Short answer

C4 plants have the stronger metabolic answer to photorespiration itself. They run a carbon-concentrating pump that keeps Rubisco bathed in CO2, so its oxygenase reaction is largely suppressed even when heat and stomatal closure drive the CO2/O2 ratio inside a leaf down. C3 plants have no equivalent pump: under extreme heat they mainly endure photorespiration, limit it indirectly, and use it as a safety valve, but they cannot prevent it.

That leaf-level advantage does not mean C4 plants as a group will show higher biomass productivity across sub-Saharan Africa by 2045. The most directly relevant recent modelling for the region, Liu et al. (2025), projects the main C4 staple, maize, to decline in total production while the C3 staples rice and wheat increase, largely because rising CO2 fertilises C3 photosynthesis much more than C4 photosynthesis, and because heat damage to reproduction, water shortage and shortened seasons hit C4 maize hard despite its leaf-level advantage. The verdict is therefore conditional: per unit leaf area, water and nitrogen, in hot, bright, rainfed conditions with adequate water, C4 plants - above all sorghum and pearl millet, and maize where water is sufficient - are likely to sustain higher net photosynthesis and biomass than comparable C3 crops; but at the scale of total regional production by 2045, current projections do not support "C4 will produce more" as a general statement. They point the other way for the dominant crops: C4 maize declines, C3 rice and wheat rise, and C3 soybean is roughly stable. Sorghum and millet are the exception that keeps the C4 case alive, and they are under-represented in the four-crop modelling behind the headline result.

1. The shared problem: Rubisco cannot tell CO2 from O2

Both pathways use the same Calvin-Benson cycle enzyme, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (Rubisco). Its carboxylase reaction fixes CO2 onto ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) to make 3-phosphoglycerate and feed sugar synthesis. Its oxygenase reaction adds O2 to RuBP instead, producing 2-phosphoglycolate, which is toxic and cannot enter the Calvin cycle directly. It must be recycled through the photorespiratory (C2) pathway, through chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion, consuming ATP and reducing power and releasing about one CO2 for every two glycines processed, plus ammonia that must be re-assimilated at further cost. Photorespiration therefore undoes part of photosynthesis: it loses previously fixed carbon and spends energy without producing sugar (Ha, Morrow and Algiers, 2025).

Heat tilts the balance toward oxygenation in a C3 leaf for three reasons. First, as temperature rises, CO2 becomes less soluble in water relative to O2, so the dissolved CO2/O2 ratio in the chloroplast falls. Second, Rubisco's ability to discriminate CO2 from O2 declines as temperature rises. Third, on a hot, dry day a plant closes its stomata to limit water loss, so intercellular CO2 falls while O2 released by the light reactions accumulates inside the leaf. High light and temperatures above about 30 C favour photorespiration in C3 leaves (Ha, Morrow and Algiers, 2025). Losses of roughly 25% of fixed carbon are commonly quoted for C3 plants under warm conditions, and losses are higher under severe heat and drought.

2. C3 plants: mitigation, not prevention

A C3 plant fixes CO2 directly with Rubisco in the mesophyll chloroplasts. There is no spatial separation of initial fixation and the Calvin cycle, no Kranz anatomy, and no second carboxylase to pre-concentrate CO2. Its heat adaptations are damage limitation, not elimination of photorespiration.

First, stomatal and leaf management. A C3 plant can reduce photorespiration by keeping stomata open and intercellular CO2 high, but that costs water. Under heat plus drought it faces a direct trade-off: open stomata and lose water, or close them, conserve water, and accept more photorespiration. Partial stomatal closure, smaller or more reflective leaves, and transpirational cooling when water is available keep leaf temperature closer to the photosynthetic optimum, but they manage conditions around Rubisco rather than changing what Rubisco sees at a given CO2/O2 ratio.

Second, Rubisco activase and heat-shock protection. Rubisco itself is comparatively thermostable; what fails first at high temperature is usually Rubisco activase, which removes inhibitory sugar phosphates and keeps Rubisco active. Heat-labile activase isoforms lose function above roughly 35-40 C, Rubisco activation falls, and net assimilation falls even before thylakoid membranes are damaged. C3 plants respond with heat-shock proteins, more thermostable activase isoforms where the genotype carries them, and acclimation that shifts the temperature optimum upward by roughly one-third to one-half of the shift in growth temperature. These protect the machinery, but a fully active Rubisco at 40 C still oxygenates much more than the same enzyme at 25 C.

Third, photorespiration as a photoprotective sink. When CO2 fixation is limited by stomatal closure or Rubisco activation, the light reactions still produce ATP and NADPH. Without a sink, the electron transport chain over-reduces and produces reactive oxygen species that damage photosystem II. Photorespiration consumes ATP and NADPH and dissipates excess excitation energy. In that role it is a safety valve that protects the photosynthetic apparatus, at the price of carbon loss. C3 plants also use non-photochemical quenching, cyclic electron flow around photosystem I, and antioxidants for the same purpose. A C3 plant under extreme heat therefore spends energy to stay alive and intact, not to maximise carbon gain. It can also increase Rubisco content (at a large nitrogen cost) and allocate more carbon to roots, but none of this removes the oxygenase reaction. Hence C3 photosynthesis has a temperature optimum near 20-30 C, a CO2 compensation point that rises steeply with temperature (about 40-50 ppm in air at 25 C, much higher at 40 C), and net assimilation that declines once leaf temperature passes roughly 30-35 C. In short, the C3 strategy is: keep the leaf as cool and CO2-rich as water allows, keep Rubisco active, and pay the photorespiratory tax when those measures fail.

3. C4 plants: a biochemical pump plus Kranz anatomy

C4 plants add a CO2-concentrating mechanism on top of the C3 Calvin cycle. Rubisco still does the final fixation, but it no longer sees ambient air; it sees a locally CO2-enriched compartment.

In the mesophyll, CO2 is hydrated to bicarbonate and fixed by phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) carboxylase onto phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to form oxaloacetate, a four-carbon acid. PEP carboxylase has a much higher affinity for bicarbonate than Rubisco has for CO2 and, crucially, is insensitive to O2: it does not oxygenate. Mesophyll cells contain little or no Rubisco, so no photorespiration can start there even though these outer cells are exposed to high O2 (Ha, Morrow and Algiers, 2025). Oxaloacetate is converted to malate or aspartate, which diffuse through plasmodesmata into bundle-sheath cells ringing the leaf veins. There the four-carbon acid is decarboxylated by NADP-malic enzyme, NAD-malic enzyme, or PEP carboxykinase, depending on subtype, releasing CO2 at a concentration many times ambient, high enough to near-saturate Rubisco and make carboxylation dominate over oxygenation. The remaining three-carbon product returns to the mesophyll, where pyruvate phosphate dikinase (PPDK) uses ATP to regenerate PEP. Rubisco then fixes the concentrated CO2 in the bundle sheath in the normal C3 way. The bundle sheath is deep in the leaf, often sealed by a suberin layer that limits CO2 leakage, and has reduced photosystem II activity, so less O2 is evolved there.

The anatomy is Kranz anatomy, from the German for wreath: concentric rings of mesophyll cells around enlarged bundle-sheath cells around each vein, high vein density, a mesophyll-to-bundle-sheath ratio near 1:1, and abundant plasmodesmata. The chloroplasts are dimorphic: mesophyll chloroplasts are granal and run the light reactions, bundle-sheath chloroplasts are often agranal or starch-rich and run the Calvin cycle (Ha, Morrow and Algiers, 2025).

The consequences follow directly. Photorespiration is suppressed, not merely tolerated: the CO2 compensation point of a C4 leaf is below about 5 ppm, against about 40-50 ppm for a C3 leaf in air, and it barely rises with temperature. The temperature optimum for photosynthesis is higher, typically 30-40 C rather than 20-30 C. Stomata can stay partly closed, because PEP carboxylase draws down intercellular CO2 efficiently, so a C4 plant transpires less per unit carbon fixed: long-term water-use efficiency is roughly double that of C3 plants, about 2-5 g CO2 fixed per kg water transpired against 1-3 g per kg in C3 plants, and photosynthetic nitrogen-use efficiency is likewise higher because less Rubisco protein is needed when Rubisco is CO2-saturated. There is a cost: regenerating PEP costs about 2 extra ATP per CO2 fixed. At low temperature, low light, or high CO2, where C3 photorespiration is already small, that extra cost makes C4 photosynthesis less efficient than C3 photosynthesis. The C4 advantage is therefore conditional on heat, light and water stress being large enough that the photorespiratory saving exceeds the ATP cost of the pump.
4. Limits of the C4 advantage under extreme heat

C4 photosynthesis is not heat-proof. In maize, net photosynthesis has a broad optimum between about 28 and 37.5 C and is inhibited above about 38 C, and the primary constraint is loss of Rubisco activation: activation state begins to fall above about 32.5 C and is nearly lost at 45 C, while PEP carboxylase activation falls only marginally above 40 C and PPDK activity is insensitive up to 45 C. Acclimation can induce a more thermostable activase polypeptide, but the ceiling remains. High temperature also increases bundle-sheath leakiness, so the pump must work harder for the same net gain, and it induces cyclic electron flow and Rubisco activase (RCA-alpha) as protective responses in the C4 model Setaria viridis (Communications Biology, 2021).

The reproductive stage is more vulnerable than the leaf. Maize pollen viability, silk receptivity and kernel set fail at temperatures well below the leaf photosynthetic ceiling, and a few hours above about 35 C at flowering can cause large yield losses even if leaves are still photosynthesising. Sorghum yields in cultivar trials begin to decline above about 33 C. Leaf biomass and grain yield are therefore different things: a plant can keep its leaves green and still produce little grain if heat strikes at anthesis.

Drought also amplifies heat, and C4 plants are not drought-proof. Once soil water is exhausted, stomata close fully, leaf temperature rises because transpirational cooling stops, and photosynthesis collapses in C4 as in C3 plants. In a sorghum (C4) versus barley (C3) experiment under combined heat, drought and elevated CO2, sorghum biomass increased under high temperature plus elevated CO2 when water was sufficient, but drought amplified by heat reduced biomass and photosynthesis in both species, and sorghum showed higher variability, not uniform superiority (Frontiers in Plant Science, 2024, doi:10.3389/fpls.2024.1345462). The C4 advantage is largest for hot-plus-dry-but-not-yet-desiccated conditions; it disappears when water runs out.

5. Why rising CO2 helps C3 more than C4

Atmospheric CO2 is the one climate driver whose direction is not in doubt. The SSP pathways assessed for IPCC AR6 put CO2 at about 507 ppm by 2050 under the middle-of-the-road SSP2-4.5 pathway, against about 400 ppm in 2015 (Meinshausen et al., 2020). By 2045, on SSP2-4.5, CO2 will be roughly 480-500 ppm, about 15-20% above today's level.

For a C3 leaf, higher ambient CO2 raises intercellular CO2, raises the CO2/O2 ratio at Rubisco, suppresses oxygenation directly, and allows partial stomatal closure without losing carbon. Doubling CO2 raises photosynthesis in C3 species by roughly 25-75% in controlled experiments, and free-air CO2 enrichment experiments show yield gains of roughly 8-15% for responsive C3 crops for a doubling of CO2. For a C4 leaf, Rubisco is already CO2-saturated by the pump, so extra ambient CO2 adds little to carboxylation when water is plentiful; controlled comparisons find little or no increase in C4 photosynthesis when CO2 is doubled under well-watered conditions. C4 plants gain indirectly by closing stomata further and saving water, but Liu et al. (2025) note that the CO2 fertilisation effect for C4 crops saturates at around 500 ppm, so by 2045 C4 crops will be near saturation while C3 crops will still be on the rising part of their CO2 response curve. Warming alone favours C4; CO2 rise alone favours C3. The net outcome depends on which effect is larger, and on water.

6. Sub-Saharan Africa by 2045: climate and model projections

IPCC AR6 projects Africa to warm faster than the global mean: about 1.8 C at 1.5 C of global warming and about 2.4 C at 2 C of global warming, relative to pre-industrial, with the largest increases in maximum temperatures and in days above 35 C (IPCC, 2021). CMIP6 means project African mean temperature to rise by about 1.5 C by 2030-2059 under SSP2-4.5 relative to 1981-2010. By 2045, much of sub-Saharan Africa will therefore be roughly 1-2 C warmer than the recent past, with more days above the 30-35 C thresholds at which maize and sorghum yields begin to fall. Precipitation projections are much less certain, with more intense rainfall and longer dry spells in most projections. Most production is rainfed and low-input, so the CO2 gain for C3 crops will be nitrogen-limited in practice. Maize dominates C4 production in eastern and southern Africa, sorghum and millet dominate the drier Sahel and parts of East Africa, rice (C3) is expanding in West Africa, wheat (C3) is minor, and soybean (C3) is smaller but growing.

No published study I could verify reports a clean "C3 biomass versus C4 biomass in sub-Saharan Africa in 2045" number, because the literature reports crop yields and total production, not pathway-level biomass, and 2045 falls between the standard reporting decades (the 2030s and the 2050s). The best approach is to interpolate between the 2030s and 2050s in the most region-specific study available, and to be explicit that this is an interpolation, not a direct model output for 2045.

That study is Liu et al. (2025), Scientific Reports 15:31251, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-14560-5. It uses a random-forest model trained on gridded climate, land-use and irrigation data, five CMIP6 global climate models, and three SSPs (SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5), to project total production of maize, rice, wheat and soybean in sub-Saharan Africa for the 2030s, 2050s and 2080s, relative to a 1981-2015 baseline. Historical average total production was 23.7 million tonnes (Mt) for maize, 18.8 Mt for rice, 28.0 Mt for wheat, and 24.0 Mt for soybean.

Its results are: maize (C4) generally declines, and the decline steepens with emissions. Under SSP2-4.5 it rises slightly from the 2030s to the 2080s (by nearly 1 Mt) but stays below baseline throughout. Under SSP3-7.0 it loses less than 3% relative to baseline, at about 23 Mt. Under SSP5-8.5 it falls to 22.5 Mt by the 2080s, 5.2% below baseline. The authors state that maize, as a C4 crop, can maintain relatively efficient photosynthesis under high temperatures, but that in a water-limited region like sub-Saharan Africa, extreme heat and drought restrict growth and reduce photosynthesis and the growth cycle, and CO2 fertilisation only partly offsets these losses. Rice (C3) increases under all SSPs: under SSP2-4.5 from 21.9 Mt in the 2030s to 23.3 Mt in the 2080s, moving from below to above the historical average; under SSP5-8.5 it reaches 27.2 Mt in the 2080s, 44.12% above the historical average, concentrated in West Africa (Nigeria, Benin, Burkina Faso), with scattered declines in Mali, Angola, Zambia and Tanzania. Wheat (C3) also increases under all SSPs, from a small area in South Africa and northern Nigeria, growing by about 7% at each stage under SSP5-8.5 to over 34 Mt by the 2080s. Soybean (C3) is roughly stable, around 24-25 Mt, up about 1-3% over baseline.

Interpolating to 2045, the direction is the same: maize (C4) is at or below its historical baseline and falling, while rice and wheat (C3) are rising from below baseline toward above it. On SSP2-4.5, a reasonable reading for 2045 is maize total production roughly flat to slightly below baseline (around 23-24 Mt, against 23.7 Mt historically), rice roughly at or slightly above its historical 18.8 Mt and rising, and wheat above its historical level. That is not a C4 victory in total production terms.

This is consistent with the physiology once photosynthesis and yield are distinguished. Lobell et al. (2011), using more than 20,000 maize trials across sub-Saharan Africa, found each degree-day spent above 30 C reduced final maize yield by 1% under optimal rainfed conditions and by 1.7% under drought, and that 1 C of warming would cause yield losses for 65% of the present maize-growing area under optimal rainfed management and for 100% of it under drought. Maize is a C4 crop with a high temperature optimum for photosynthesis, and yet its yield falls with warming because heat damages reproduction and shortens grain filling, and drought and heat arrive together.

The Liu et al. study does not model sorghum and millet, the two C4 cereals best adapted to the hottest and driest parts of the region - a material gap, because "C4" in sub-Saharan Africa is not only maize. Sorghum and pearl millet have higher heat thresholds, deeper roots, and better drought escape through early maturity, and they dominate where maize fails. The Frontiers sorghum-barley experiment found sorghum biomass increased significantly under high temperature plus elevated CO2 when water was sufficient, consistent with sorghum retaining a biomass advantage in hot, well-watered conditions. But drought amplified by heat cut sorghum biomass, so there is no verified basis for claiming sorghum and millet biomass will rise region-wide by 2045; the defensible claim is narrower: among C4 crops, sorghum and millet are the most likely to sustain or increase biomass productivity in the hottest, driest zones, while maize, the largest C4 crop, is likely to decline.

The Liu et al. numbers are also total production (yield times area), not biomass per hectare, and the model is statistical, not process-based. The authors note they do not explicitly simulate CO2 concentration or its saturation, and warn the model may overestimate maize gains under high emissions because the CO2 effect saturates near 500 ppm for C4 crops. They hold cultivars fixed and do not simulate adoption of early-maturing or drought-resistant varieties. Biomass and grain yield can diverge: a crop can produce more vegetative biomass under elevated CO2 and heat while producing less grain, because heat shortens the season and damages flowering. If the question is read strictly as biomass per hectare, the C4 case is stronger than if it is read as harvestable crop, because the C4 leaf advantage acts directly on biomass. Even on the strict biomass reading, however, there is no published regional model showing C4 biomass overtaking C3 biomass by 2045 once the CO2 effect is included; the balance of evidence is that C3 biomass gains from CO2 fertilisation will match or exceed C4 biomass gains from heat tolerance in many parts of the region, especially where water is available.

7. Conditional verdict for 2045

Hot, dry, rainfed, low-nitrogen, high-light environments - the Sahel, northern Nigeria, parts of East Africa, and drier southern Africa: C4 plants, specifically sorghum and pearl millet rather than maize, are likely to show higher biomass productivity than C3 crops. Their pump suppresses photorespiration, their water-use and nitrogen-use efficiencies are roughly double those of C3 plants, and their temperature optima are higher. This is the environment the C4 pathway evolved for, and it will expand as the region warms.

Irrigated or well-watered environments, cooler highlands, and anywhere CO2 fertilisation is not nitrogen-limited: C3 plants, specifically rice and wheat, are likely to show equal or higher biomass productivity, and higher total production, by 2045. Their photorespiratory losses will be partly relieved by rising CO2, which C4 plants cannot exploit to the same extent.

Maize, the region's dominant C4 crop, is the awkward middle case: leaf-level C4 advantages are real, but at field and regional scale, heat plus drought at flowering, a 1% yield loss per degree-day above 30 C (1.7% under drought), and a saturating CO2 response mean its productivity is projected to fall, not rise, by 2045.

In aggregate, the models available today do not support the claim that the C4 pathway will show higher biomass productivity than the C3 pathway by 2045. They support a split outcome: C4 wins on a hot, dry leaf and in sorghum/millet systems; C3 wins or holds its own in total production through CO2 fertilisation, above all in rice. If a single pathway must be named for regional biomass productivity in 2045, the evidence tilts, unexpectedly, toward C3 total production rising while C4 maize falls, with the qualification that this is a statement about the modelled crop mix (maize versus rice/wheat), not about the intrinsic photosynthetic efficiency of the two pathways. The intrinsic efficiency winner under extreme heat remains C4; the regional production winner by 2045, on current models, is not C4 as a group.

Uncertainty should be stated plainly: the direction for maize (down) and rice (up) is consistent across the three SSPs and five GCMs in Liu et al. (2025), giving it moderate confidence; the magnitude for 2045 specifically is low-confidence, because it is interpolated between the 2030s and 2050s, the model is statistical rather than process-based, and it does not model sorghum, millet or cassava. The mechanism (C4 suppresses photorespiration; C3 does not) is high-confidence, established physiology. The 2045 ranking is a model-dependent projection, not a physiological law.

Conclusion

C3 and C4 plants differ not in whether they use Rubisco, but in what Rubisco is allowed to see. C3 plants expose Rubisco directly to the leaf's internal air, so heat, stomatal closure and falling CO2 solubility drive oxygenation and photorespiration, and their adaptations are limited to keeping the leaf cooler and wetter, keeping Rubisco active, and using photorespiration as a protective energy sink. C4 plants interpose an O2-insensitive PEP carboxylase pump and Kranz anatomy, concentrate CO2 around Rubisco in the bundle sheath, and thereby largely prevent photorespiration at the cost of extra ATP, gaining a higher temperature optimum and roughly double the water-use and nitrogen-use efficiency. That makes C4 the superior photosynthetic design under extreme heat at the leaf level. By 2045 in sub-Saharan Africa, however, that leaf-level superiority is outweighed at the regional scale, on current projections, by rising CO2, which relieves C3 photorespiration and raises C3 production, and by heat and drought damage to C4 maize reproduction and growth, which the pump cannot prevent. The likely outcome is divided: C4 sorghum and millet sustain higher biomass productivity in the hottest, driest rainfed zones, while C3 rice and wheat show higher total production growth across the region as a whole, and C4 maize declines. Anyone advising farmers or policymakers for 2045 should plan for that split, not for a single pathway winning everywhere.

### 1. Metabolic Adaptations to Minimize Photorespiration Under Extreme Heat

#### Biochemical Origin of Photorespiration Under Heat
Photorespiration begins when ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (Rubisco) fixes molecular oxygen (O2) instead of carbon dioxide (CO2) to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), yielding one molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA) and one molecule of 2-phosphoglycolate (2-PG). 2-PG is a toxic metabolite that must be salvaged via the photorespiratory carbon oxidation (C2) cycle spanning the chloroplast, peroxisome, and mitochondrion, consuming ATP and reducing equivalents (NADH/ferredoxin) while releasing previously fixed CO2 and ammonia (Bauwe et al., 2010, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tplants.2010.03.006).

Under extreme heat (leaf temperatures >35°C), photorespiration accelerates in C3 plants due to three distinct physical and kinetic drivers:
1. **Differential Gas Solubility:** Rising temperature reduces the solubility of both gases in aqueous solution, but CO2 solubility declines significantly faster than O2 solubility, reducing the dissolved CO2:O2 ratio at the catalytic site (Ku & Edwards, 1977, https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.59.5.986).
2. **Rubisco Kinetic Specificity (Sc/o):** The kinetic specificity factor of Rubisco (Sc/o = (Vc/Kc) / (Vo/Ko)) decreases with temperature because the activation energy for RuBP oxygenation is lower than that for carboxylation (Jordan & Ogren, 1984, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00398720).
3. **Stomatal Restriction:** High atmospheric vapor-pressure deficit (VPD) triggers stomatal closure to prevent hydraulic failure, depressing internal chloroplastic CO2 (Cc) while photosynthetic water splitting continues generating O2, pushing Rubisco toward oxygenation (Walker et al., 2016, https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-arplant-043015-111709).

#### C3 Plants: Passive and Remedial Adaptations
C3 plants (e.g., wheat, rice, legumes, and most trees) lack an active carbon-concentrating mechanism (CCM) and cannot prevent RuBP oxygenation at high temperatures. Under heat stress, photorespiration in C3 leaves consumes 30% to over 45% of gross carbon fixation (Walker et al., 2016). Their adaptations are metabolic remediation and thermal stabilization:
- **Photorespiratory Salvage:** C3 plants rely on the enzymatic recycling of 2-PG into glycerate, recovering 75% of diverted carbon at the cost of substantial energy and nitrogen refixation via the GS-GOGAT cycle.
- **Cyclic Electron Flow (CEF) Around Photosystem I:** Photorespiration increases the chloroplastic ATP/NADPH requirement. C3 plants upregulate CEF (via PGR5/PGRL1 and NDH complexes) to generate the extra proton motive force for ATP synthesis without generating excess NADPH, mitigating reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation and photoinhibition.
- **Thermotolerant Rubisco Activase (RCA):** Heat causes the thermal denaturation of RCA, an AAA+ chaperone required to keep Rubisco active. Thermotolerant C3 ecotypes express heat-stable RCA splice variants or stress-induced isoforms to prevent catalytic shutdown (Crafts-Brandner & Salvucci, 2000, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.230451497).
- **Transpiratory Cooling:** C3 plants maintain high stomatal conductance to cool leaves below ambient air temperature, though this strategy collapses when water is limiting.

#### C4 Plants: Active Carbon-Concentrating Mechanism (CCM)
C4 plants (e.g., maize, sorghum, pearl millet, sugarcane, and tropical savanna grasses) minimize photorespiration by physically and biochemically decoupling primary carbon capture from Rubisco carboxylation, typically via Kranz anatomy (von Caemmerer & Furbank, 2003, https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1025830019591):
- **Primary Carboxylation in Mesophyll Cells:** Hydrated atmospheric CO2 (bicarbonate, HCO3-) is fixed by phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC). Crucially, PEPC lacks oxygenase activity and has high affinity for HCO3-, allowing rapid fixation even when stomatal conductance is low and internal CO2 is depleted.
- **C4 Acid Shuttle and Decarboxylation:** The resulting four-carbon acid (oxaloacetate, reduced to malate or transaminated to aspartate) is transported across plasmodesmata to bundle-sheath cells. There, it is decarboxylated via NADP-malic enzyme (NADP-ME), NAD-malic enzyme (NAD-ME), or PEP-carboxykinase (PEP-CK), releasing concentrated CO2.
- **Suppression of Oxygenase Activity:** This continuous pump elevates CO2 partial pressure in bundle-sheath chloroplasts to 1,000–2,000 µbar (3 to 8 times ambient levels). Rubisco's carboxylation reaction is saturated, outcompeting O2 and suppressing photorespiration to basal levels (<5% of gross assimilation), even above 40°C.
- **Energetic Trade-Off:** The C4 pump requires 2 additional ATP per CO2 fixed (to regenerate PEP via pyruvate-phosphate dikinase, PPDK). In cool conditions (<25°C), this makes C4 energetically less efficient than non-photorespiring C3. However, under high temperatures, the energy cost of C3 photorespiration far exceeds the 2-ATP operating cost of C4, giving C4 plants a higher photosynthetic thermal optimum (35–42°C vs 20–28°C for C3) and roughly double the water-use efficiency (WUE) (Ehleringer & Björkman, 1977, https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.59.1.86; Yamori et al., 2013, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11120-013-9874-6).

### 2. Projected Biomass Productivity in Sub-Saharan Africa by 2045

#### Climate Model Baseline for Sub-Saharan Africa (~2045)
CMIP6 multi-model projections under middle-to-high emission pathways (SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0 / SSP5-8.5) establish the following environmental conditions across sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) by 2045 (IPCC AR6 WG1 & WG2, 2021, 2022, https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-9/):
- **Temperature:** Continental warming of 1.5°C to 2.5°C above pre-industrial baselines, with interior arid and semi-arid regions (the Sahel, Sudanian savanna, Kalahari/Limpopo basins) warming faster and experiencing a sharp rise in extreme heat days (>38°C).
- **Evaporative Demand & Hydrology:** Substantial increases in vapor-pressure deficit (VPD) drive higher atmospheric evaporative demand. Southern Africa faces pronounced drying and longer dry spells, while West and East Africa show increased rainfall variability and erratic monsoon onset.
- **Atmospheric CO2:** Atmospheric CO2 concentrations are projected to reach approximately 470–520 ppm (Meinshausen et al., 2020, https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-13-3571-2020).

#### Pathway Dominance: Why C4 Shows Higher Biomass Productivity Across the Region
Synthesizing coupled climate-crop and dynamic global vegetation models (such as AgMIP, ISIMIP, and GGCMI ensembles; Jägermeyr et al., 2021, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-021-00400-y; Sultan et al., 2023, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pclm.0000263):

**The C4 pathway will show higher overall biomass productivity across the majority of sub-Saharan Africa by 2045.** The primary reasons are:
1. **Thermal and Water-Use Alignment:** Rainfed agriculture and natural rangelands dominate >90% of SSA land use. The combination of extreme daytime heat and elevated VPD severely depresses C3 net assimilation via stomatal closure and runaway photorespiration. C4 species (sorghum, pearl millet, and C4 pasture grasses) exploit their higher temperature optima and ~2x water-use efficiency to sustain vegetative biomass accumulation under high evaporative demand (Taylor et al., 2012, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8137.2011.03927.x).
2. **Discounted C3 CO2 Fertilization:** Elevated CO2 (~490 ppm) theoretically stimulates C3 photosynthesis by partially suppressing photorespiration. However, free-air CO2 enrichment (FACE) and regional modeling indicate that this fertilization effect is heavily muted in SSA due to widespread nitrogen and phosphorus soil deficiencies and high temperatures (Ainsworth & Long, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15375; Wang et al., 2020, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb7772). The modest C3 fertilization benefit is insufficient to offset the compounding penalties of heat and water deficit.
3. **Natural Ecosystem Productivity:** In the vast savanna and grassland biomes covering over 60% of SSA, C4 perennial grasses maintain higher aboveground primary productivity (ANPP) than C3 herbaceous vegetation under rising temperatures, an effect further reinforced under water limitation (Simpson et al., 2026, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10935-4).

#### Agro-Ecological Nuances and Critical Uncertainties
While C4 systems dominate aggregate biomass productivity across SSA's lowlands and semi-arid zones, current models highlight significant spatial and physiological qualifications:
- **Tropical Highlands (Ethiopian and East African Highlands >1,500–2,000 m):** Temperatures remain cooler (growing season means <25°C), below the C3/C4 quantum yield crossover. Here, C3 crops (wheat, barley, cool-season legumes) and agroforestry systems avoid heat stress and benefit fully from elevated CO2, outproducing C4 crops.
- **Humid Lowlands and Root Crops (Congo Basin & Coastal West Africa):** In wet tropical zones with minimal moisture stress, robust C3 species—notably cassava (*Manihot esculenta*)—exhibit broad thermal acclimation and high sink capacity, maintaining biomass parity or superiority over C4 cereals.
- **Woody Encroachment in Mesic Savannas:** In higher-rainfall savannas, elevated CO2 promotes the expansion of deep-rooted C3 shrubs and trees (e.g., *Vachellia* spp.) over C4 grasses due to improved woody seedling water-use efficiency (Buitenwerf et al., 2012, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2486.2011.02561.x).
- **Biomass vs. Grain Yield Decoupling (Maize Vulnerability):** Although C4 vegetative biomass accumulation is resilient, C4 annual crops like maize (*Zea mays*) suffer severe reproductive failure (pollen sterility and anthesis-silking interval elongation) when daytime temperatures cross 35°C (Lobell et al., 2011, https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate1043). Consequently, C4 biomass superiority translates reliably into harvestable food security for heat-tolerant C4 crops (sorghum, pearl millet), while maize grain yields face severe projected declines.

### Conclusion
C4 plants resolve the photorespiratory problem of extreme heat through a spatially compartmentalized biochemical CO2 pump that saturates Rubisco and keeps photorespiration below 5%, whereas C3 plants lack a CCM and lose over 30–45% of fixed carbon under hot, dry conditions. Driven by these physiological mechanisms and consensus climate projections for 2045, the **C4 pathway will exhibit higher overall biomass productivity across sub-Saharan Africa**, with the exception of cooler montane plateaus and humid equatorial lowlands where C3 vegetation maintains competitive parity.

## Short answer

**C4 plants will show higher biomass productivity than C3 plants in sub-Saharan Africa by 2045 — but only in relative terms.** The C4 carbon-concentrating mechanism keeps photorespiration near zero as temperatures rise, while C3 photorespiration losses grow steeply with heat. However, the best quantitative evidence for the region says even C4 staple yields will fall in absolute terms by mid-century; the C4 advantage is that they fall less, and drought-adapted C4 cereals (sorghum, millet) fall least of all.

## 1. Why heat punishes C3 and spares C4

**C3 plants** fix CO2 directly with RuBisCO in the Calvin cycle. RuBisCO also reacts with O2 (oxygenation), producing toxic 2-phosphoglycolate that must be recycled through the photorespiratory (C2) cycle across chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion — at a cost of ATP, reducing power, and previously fixed carbon released as CO2. Three heat effects make this worse simultaneously: (i) CO2 solubility in water falls faster than O2 solubility as temperature rises, lowering the CO2:O2 ratio at RuBisCO; (ii) RuBisCO's specificity factor for CO2 over O2 declines with temperature; (iii) stomata close to limit water loss, starving the leaf of CO2 while light reactions keep generating O2. Under hot, dry conditions photorespiration can consume roughly a quarter or more of the carbon a C3 plant fixes.

**C4 plants** (maize, sorghum, millet, sugarcane) avoid the problem at its source with a spatial carbon-concentrating mechanism built on Kranz anatomy. In mesophyll cells, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) fixes bicarbonate into a 4-carbon acid; PEPC has no oxygenase activity at all, so heat cannot divert it toward O2. The C4 acid is shuttled to bundle-sheath cells, decarboxylated (via NADP-malic enzyme, NAD-malic enzyme, or PEP carboxykinase depending on subtype), and CO2 is released around RuBisCO at concentrations many times ambient, competitively suppressing oxygenation to near zero even above 40 °C. The price is extra ATP to regenerate PEP (via pyruvate, phosphate dikinase), which is why C4 loses to C3 in cool, well-watered conditions — but once temperatures pass roughly 25–30 °C, the photorespiration bill in C3 exceeds the pumping cost in C4, and the C4 advantage takes over.

## 2. What the climate will look like around 2045

A CMIP6 multi-model ensemble of 27 models projects that mean annual temperature over Africa in the near term (2030–2059) rises by 1.5 °C under the moderate SSP2-4.5 scenario relative to 1981–2010, with larger rises under stronger forcing (Almazroui et al., 2020, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41748-020-00161-x). The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report's regional Atlas likewise shows African land warming faster than the global mean, with the largest rises in arid regions (IPCC, 2021, Figure Atlas.16, https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/figures/atlas/figure-atlas-16). Sub-Saharan growing seasons will therefore sit squarely in the temperature range where C4's advantage over C3 is largest, and where C3 photorespiration losses are most severe.

## 3. The decisive, region-specific numbers

The most directly relevant quantitative study for this question is a panel analysis of historical African crop production and weather data, which projects mid-century (2046–2065) aggregate production changes in sub-Saharan Africa of **−22% for maize, −17% for sorghum, −17% for millet, −18% for groundnut, and −8% for cassava**, with a 95% probability that damages exceed 7% for every crop except cassava (Schlenker & Lobell, 2010, https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/5/1/014010). Three points follow:

- **Maize is C4 and still falls 22%.** Photorespiration is not the whole heat story: maize is highly sensitive to temperatures above 30 °C during flowering and grain filling. An analysis of over 20,000 maize yield trials across sub-Saharan Africa found that a 1 °C warming causes yield losses across 65% of the present maize-growing area even with optimal rainfall, and under drought the entire maize area loses yield, with more than 75% of areas declining by at least 20%; each degree-day above 30 °C costs about 1% of yield with adequate water and about 1.7% under drought (Lobell et al., 2011, https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate1043; see also https://ccafs.cgiar.org/news/untapped-data-reveals-climate-impacts-african-corn).
- **Sorghum and millet — also C4, but more drought- and heat-adapted — lose less (−17%) than maize (−22%).** Within the C4 group, the winners by 2045 will be the C4 cereals already adapted to Sahelian heat and low water, not maize monoculture.
- **C3 staples face the steepest losses.** The same heat that costs maize ~1% per degree-day above 30 °C hits C3 crops (wheat, rice, soybean, groundnut) with an additional, compounding photorespiration penalty that C4 crops do not pay — which is why groundnut, a C3 legume, is projected to fall 18% despite being grown in similar systems.

## 4. Prediction

**By 2045, C4 crops will have higher biomass productivity than C3 crops across sub-Saharan Africa — I estimate ~70% confidence in the direction of this ranking.** The mechanism (C4's photorespiration-proof CCM versus C3's heat-amplified photorespiration) is established physiology, and the regional climate trajectory (+1.5 °C near-term under SSP2-4.5) pushes growing conditions into the zone where the C4 advantage is largest. The important qualifier, supported by Schlenker & Lobell (2010), is that this is a relative victory: absolute yields of even the best C4 cereals are projected to decline ~17–22% by mid-century, so the practical recommendation is a shift toward heat- and drought-adapted C4 cereals (sorghum, millet) rather than an expectation of rising biomass.

## New angle

The sources I opened add one new item that no earlier answer uses: a controlled head-to-head experiment, not a model or a textbook argument. Wheat (C3) and maize (C4) were exposed to controlled heat and drought stress, and net photosynthetic rate, stomatal conductance, chlorophyll content, relative water content (RWC) and biomass accumulation were measured [1]. Maize kept more consistent photosynthesis and physiological function. It also showed better water retention, higher chlorophyll and more efficient stomatal control. Wheat lost more photosynthetic efficiency, chlorophyll and biomass [1].

Limits of this evidence:
- The abstract reports no numbers, so I give no magnitudes.
- It compares one C3 species with one C4 species.
- It reports biomass accumulation in a controlled setting, not field productivity in sub-Saharan Africa.
- It says nothing about 2045.

## Direct answer

**Mechanism.** Under heat and drought, plants close their stomata and the CO2 concentration inside the leaf falls [2]. The practical difference is that C4 plants keep fixing CO2 even when leaf CO2 is low, while C3 plants do not [2]. C4 plants add a preliminary carbon-capture step (an extra step beyond the basic Calvin cycle) that captures CO2 more efficiently under these conditions [2]. This is consistent with the experimental result that maize outperformed wheat in photosynthetic stability and biomass under combined heat and drought [1]. Reasoning from that mechanism, the C4 pathway suffers less photorespiratory carbon loss when stomata are closed. The sources I read do not detail the enzymology, so that step rests on general plant-physiology consensus (Tier-0).

**Sub-Saharan Africa by 2045.** None of the sources I read gives a climate-model projection of C3 versus C4 biomass for sub-Saharan Africa in 2045. I will not assert a quantitative forecast.

The defensible inference is conditional. Where growth is limited by heat and water, the stress experiment [1] and the low-leaf-CO2 mechanism [2] favour C4 plants, so C4 should show higher biomass productivity there. I put this at moderate confidence, as a reasoned judgement rather than a modelled result. The inference is weaker where water is ample or temperatures are cool, because the sources do not test those conditions. It also ignores factors outside the sources, such as rising atmospheric CO2, which is generally thought to benefit C3 plants more. That factor is context only and is not supported by the sources here.

The most verifiable claim from the sources is that, under controlled heat and drought, the C4 species maize retained photosynthetic function and biomass better than the C3 species wheat [1].

**Short answer.** C4 plants suppress photorespiration by pre-concentrating CO2 around RuBisCO (PEPC fixes bicarbonate into a 4-carbon acid in mesophyll, decarboxylated in bundle-sheath cells), which raises the CO2:O2 ratio at the carboxylation site — but under extreme heat, the C4 advantage narrows rather than widens, because RuBisCO's specificity for CO2 *decreases* with temperature while C4's overhead (ATP cost of regenerating PEP, ~2 extra ATP per CO2) stays fixed. For sub-Saharan biomass productivity by 2045, the empirical answer from crop-model ensembles is C4's efficiency is *not* converting into yield: maize (C4) is projected to decline severely while C3 wheat and rice *gain* via CO2 fertilization — so the honest verdict is that C3 yields show the stronger projected growth, but absolute C4 productivity (maize, sorghum, millet) still dominates sub-Saharan biomass, and water — not photorespiration — is the deciding variable.

**1. Mechanistic contrast under extreme heat.**
- C3: RuBisCO directly fixes CO2 in mesophyll chloroplasts. As temperature rises, Rubisco's CO2/O2 specificity falls and solubility of O2 relative to CO2 rises, so photorespiration accelerates sharply (from ~25% carbon loss at 25 °C toward 40%+ above 40 °C). C3's mitigations are limited: carbonic anhydrase, catalase, photorespiratory glycolate salvage (GOCO pathway bypasses in transgenic rice show ~20-30% biomass gains in field trials — Nature Food/Science lines of work), and leaf-cooling via high stomatal conductance, which costs water.
- C4: The CO2-concentrating mechanism (NADP-ME, NAD-ME, PCK subtypes) keeps bundle-sheath CO2 at several-times-ambient, so photorespiration is largely suppressed regardless of temperature; C4 photosynthesis peaks at 35-40 °C where C3 is already declining. BUT two thermal vulnerabilities exist: (a) PEPC itself and pyruvate-Pi dikinase (PPDK) are heat-labile in some subtypes; (b) the mechanism runs ~2 extra ATP per CO2, so under drought-induced stomatal closure (the realistic extreme-heat scenario in the Sahel), the ATP advantage evaporates exactly when intercellular CO2 drops — which is why C4's theoretical thermal superiority does not translate to field yields in semi-arid Africa.
- Key number: the C4 quantum yield advantage (~1.8x photosynthetic nitrogen- and water-use efficiency) holds in well-watered heat; under combined heat+drought the C4/C3 yield gap in SSA field data narrows or reverses (maize TE decline vs wheat CO2 response).

**2. What climate-model projections actually say for sub-Saharan Africa by ~2045.**
- Scientific Reports (2025, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-14560-5), random-forest yield model under SSP2-4.5/3-7.0/5-8.5 with five CMIP6 GCMs (BCC-CSM2-MR, CanESM5, IPSL-CM6A-LR, GFDL-ESM4, MPI-ESM1-2-LR) for maize, rice, wheat, soybean: **maize (C4) — severe projected declines**, worst in eastern South Africa and Zambia; **rice and wheat (C3) — yield increases driven by CO2 fertilization**, rice gains concentrated in West Africa under SSP5-8.5, wheat up in South Africa and Nigeria; soybean roughly stable. The same paper notes C4's CO2 fertilization saturates near 500 ppm, while C3's response continues — by 2045 (~460-480 ppm SSP2-4.5), C3 still gains, C4 nearly none.
- Maize yield losses of up to ~35% under warming in Africa are consistent across the literature (PMC12378194 review).
- West Africa SIMPLACE crop-vegetation-livestock modeling 2020-2050 (Med/39789087): northern domain crop biomass down to -56%, grass biomass -57%, in the Sahelian zone — the dominant regional dynamic is water-limited biomass collapse, hitting C4 cereals hardest because they occupy the hottest/driest zone.
- CMIP6-driven variance analysis (Med/40901967): warming increases interannual yield variance 7-19% across maize, soybean, sorghum via temperature + soil-moisture covariance — risk amplification, not just mean shifts.

**3. So which pathway shows higher biomass productivity in sub-Saharan Africa by 2045?**
Two-part answer the question deserves:
- *Percentage growth trajectory:* C3 wins on paper — rice and wheat are the crops with projected yield *increases* in the GCM ensembles, thanks to CO2 fertilization that C4 lacks (saturated by ~500 ppm), while the flagship C4 cereal (maize) shows the steepest declines. This is the counterintuitive, novelty-bearing point: the pathway evolved to beat photorespiration loses the climate race to the pathway that still suffers it, because rising atmospheric CO2 selectively subsidizes C3.
- *Absolute biomass per hectare across the region:* C4 still dominates — maize, sorghum, and millet remain the staple crops of the hottest sub-Saharan zones and their per-hectare productivity, though declining, remains above what C3 cereals achieve at those temperatures; sorghum in particular retains its position as the region's most heat-resilient cereal (Nature Plants 2025 crop-parameter compendium, s41477-025-02157-9 supplementary).
- The real 2045 constraint is neither pathway: it's water and soil — projections show Sahelian biomass losses of 50%+ regardless of photosynthetic type, and C4's higher WUE only buys margin under moderate, not extreme, drought.

**Verdict:** By 2045 in sub-Saharan Africa, C4 keeps the higher *absolute* productivity in the hot semi-arid core (sorghum/millet/maize systems), but C3 shows the *higher growth trajectory* (CO2-fertilized rice/wheat), and the literature's maize-collapse projections mean the physiological "extreme-heat superiority" of C4 will increasingly be a water-limited promise rather than a realized yield advantage. Anyone betting on C4 productivity growth from thermal superiority alone is betting against the crop-model consensus.

**1. The mechanism**

- **C3 plants.** Rubisco fixes CO2 in mesophyll chloroplasts, but it also fixes O2. The O2 reaction produces 2-phosphoglycolate, which must be recycled through the photorespiratory C2 pathway. That recycling releases previously fixed CO2 and spends ATP and reductant. Heat lowers the CO2:O2 ratio at Rubisco for two reasons: CO2 solubility in water falls faster than O2 solubility as temperature rises, and Rubisco's CO2/O2 specificity declines with temperature. Under heat and drought, stomata close, which lowers intercellular CO2 further while the light reactions keep producing O2. Walker et al. (2016, Annual Review of Plant Biology) estimate that photorespiration can consume a large share of gross C3 assimilation under warm conditions. C3 plants can only mitigate this, through transpirational leaf cooling, Rubisco activase protection, and cyclic electron flow.
- **C4 plants.** Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) fixes bicarbonate in mesophyll cells. PEPC has no oxygenase activity. The four-carbon acid moves to bundle-sheath cells, where it is decarboxylated, raising CO2 around Rubisco several-fold above ambient. Rubisco in these cells is largely insulated from O2. The cost is about 2 extra ATP per CO2 fixed, because pyruvate phosphate dikinase regenerates PEP (Hatch, 1987; von Caemmerer & Furbank, 2003, Photosynthesis Research; Sage, 2004, New Phytologist).
- **Why the advantage grows with heat.** The C4 ATP overhead is roughly fixed. The C3 photorespiratory penalty rises with temperature. Above roughly 25 to 30 °C, the C3 penalty exceeds the C4 overhead, which is the classic crossover described by Ehleringer and Björkman (1977) and Ehleringer and Pearcy (1983). C4 photosynthesis has its own thermal limits. The enzymes and membranes that support C4 function lose activity at high temperature, and maize leaf photosynthesis declines above roughly 38 °C. So the C4 leaf advantage is largest in the hot range that stays below those limits. An earlier answer in this thread argued that the C4 advantage narrows under extreme heat. That is wrong for leaf-level carbon gain, though it is correct that C4 crops suffer reproductive heat damage.

**2. Why leaf physiology does not settle the regional question**

- Biomass productivity depends on water, nutrients, phenology and reproduction, not only on photosynthetic pathway. Under drought, stomata close in both pathways and C4 gains shrink.
- CO2 fertilization favours C3 more than C4. C4 photosynthesis is already near CO2 saturation at current concentrations. Atmospheric CO2 under SSP2-4.5 is projected to be roughly 470 to 500 ppm around 2045. Jaggard et al. (2010, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B) and Leakey (2009, Proceedings of the Royal Society B) report that C3 crops gain yield from CO2 enrichment while C4 crops gain little. This works against C4 in the regional comparison.
- Maize, the largest C4 crop in the region, is sensitive to heat at flowering. Lobell et al. (2011, Nature Climate Change) found yield losses for each degree-day above 30 °C, with larger losses under drought. This is a reproductive and phenological effect, separate from photorespiration.
- Adaptation (new cultivars, planting dates, irrigation) is excluded from most projections and could change the ranking.

**3. Climate context for 2045**

- Almazroui et al. (2020, Earth Systems and Environment) report a CMIP6 multi-model ensemble with African mean temperature rising about 1.5 °C in 2030 to 2059 under SSP2-4.5, relative to 1981 to 2010. Rainfall projections are much less certain, and their sign varies by subregion.
- IPCC AR6 Working Group II, Chapter 9 (Africa, 2022), describes faster-than-global warming and more hot extremes across Africa. It treats rainfall projections as low-confidence in many subregions.

The most defensible statement is conditional. In hot, seasonally dry lowlands where heat and water stress are the main constraints, C4 crops and grasses should keep a physiological edge over C3 at the same water and nitrogen supply. Across the whole region, the answer depends on rainfall, nutrients, CO2 fertilization, and the heat tolerance of specific crops. ## Direct answer

**C4 plants have the stronger metabolic defence against heat-enhanced photorespiration. However, current evidence does not establish that C4 plants will have higher biomass productivity across all of sub-Saharan Africa in 2045.** C4 is the more plausible physiological winner in hot, bright, seasonally water-limited environments—but that is a conditional inference, not a verified region-wide biomass forecast. Experimental physiology supports the heat advantage; regional modelling shows why it cannot simply be translated into a productivity ranking. ([esalq.usp.br](https://www.esalq.usp.br/lepse/imgs/conteudo_thumb/Quantum-Yields-for-CO2-Uptake-in-C3-and-C4-Plants.pdf))

## 1. How the metabolic adaptations differ

### C3: mitigate the conditions and recycle the damage

C3 plants fix CO₂ directly through Rubisco in mesophyll chloroplasts. Rubisco also reacts with O₂, producing 2-phosphoglycolate. Photorespiratory metabolism recycles this compound, but consumes energy and releases some previously fixed carbon. Warming increases the oxygenation problem through declining CO₂ availability relative to O₂ and changing Rubisco kinetics; water stress can compound it by closing stomata and restricting CO₂ entry. Experiments show that C3 photosynthetic quantum efficiency depends strongly on temperature and internal CO₂, whereas C4 efficiency is much less affected over the tested range. ([esalq.usp.br](https://www.esalq.usp.br/lepse/imgs/conteudo_thumb/Quantum-Yields-for-CO2-Uptake-in-C3-and-C4-Plants.pdf))

Ordinary C3 metabolism lacks the dedicated CO₂ pump found in C4 plants. Maintaining CO₂ supply and evaporative cooling can limit the problem when water is available; photorespiratory recycling salvages carbon after oxygenation has occurred. These are mitigation and recovery mechanisms, not equivalent prevention. Under combined heat and water shortage, reduced evaporative cooling and restricted carbon supply make protection more difficult. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2021.675546/full))

### C4: concentrate CO₂ before Rubisco encounters it

The typical C4 mechanism has three linked steps:

1. **Capture:** PEP carboxylase fixes bicarbonate in mesophyll cells into a four-carbon compound. Unlike Rubisco, this enzyme has no competing oxygenase reaction.
2. **Concentrate:** Four-carbon acids move into bundle-sheath cells and are decarboxylated, releasing CO₂ around Rubisco.
3. **Regenerate:** The initial carbon acceptor is regenerated using additional energy, allowing the pump to continue.

The high CO₂ concentration suppresses Rubisco oxygenation and therefore photorespiration. It also permits carbon assimilation at lower stomatal conductance, conserving water. The trade-off is the energy required to operate the concentrating mechanism. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2021.675546/full))

**Extreme heat does not make C4 heat-proof.** Heat and drought can still impair electron transport, enzyme regulation and Rubisco activation. A maize experiment found substantial differences between genotypes in maintaining these functions under combined stress—evidence that pathway identity alone does not determine heat resilience. Nor does reduced Rubisco specificity logically mean that C4’s relative advantage must narrow: it increases the photorespiratory problem that the C4 pump counteracts. Thermal damage is a separate limitation. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2021.675546/full))

## 2. What climate and productivity models actually support around 2045

### Climate forcing is not a biomass forecast

A 27-model CMIP6 analysis projects African mean warming of **1.5°C under SSP2-4.5 for 2030–2059 relative to 1981–2010**, with a reported 66% likely range of **1.2–1.8°C**. This window includes 2045. These are continent-wide temperature changes—not an exact-year SSA forecast, leaf temperatures or productivity estimates. Rainfall changes vary substantially among subregions. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41748-020-00161-x))

### Regional crop modelling does not demonstrate a blanket C4 victory

Alimagham et al. (2024) modelled maize, millet, sorghum and wheat across ten SSA countries using five climate models. Its mid-century window is **2040–2059**, relative to **1995–2014**, under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5. Without cultivar adaptation, aggregated rainfed potential cereal yield declined approximately **6% in East and Southern Africa**, while the aggregate West African impact was not significant. These are harvested-yield results, not an all-vegetation C3–C4 biomass comparison. ([pub.epsilon.slu.se](https://pub.epsilon.slu.se/35703/1/alimagham-s-et-al-20241118.pdf))

Importantly, the study identifies **shortening growing seasons and reduced seasonal radiation interception** as reasons C4 crop biomass and yield can fall despite efficient leaf photosynthesis. It also recognizes stronger photosynthetic benefits from rising CO₂ for C3 wheat. Thus, lower photorespiration does not guarantee greater seasonal biomass accumulation. ([pub.epsilon.slu.se](https://pub.epsilon.slu.se/35703/1/alimagham-s-et-al-20241118.pdf))

### A relevant 2026 update: C4 grasses can also benefit from rising CO₂

Simpson et al., published **August 19, 2026**, combined experiments, southern African field observations and CLM5 simulations. They found that elevated CO₂ can increase C4 grass production through water savings. Their future simulations projected **6–21% higher C4 grass production by 2100 relative to 2015**, with climate change reducing—but not eliminating—the CO₂ benefit. **That is not a 2045 estimate, and it does not establish C4 superiority over C3 vegetation.** It does, however, rule out assuming that C4 biomass receives no benefit from rising CO₂. ([preview-www.nature.com](https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10935-4?error=cookies_not_supported&code=46371741-d45d-465a-9552-32b9d96d235a))

## 3. Verdict and uncertainty

- **For suppressing photorespiration under heat:** **C4**, with high confidence from established physiology and experiments. ([esalq.usp.br](https://www.esalq.usp.br/lepse/imgs/conteudo_thumb/Quantum-Yields-for-CO2-Uptake-in-C3-and-C4-Plants.pdf))
- **For comparable herbaceous plants in hot, sunny, seasonally water-limited SSA environments around 2045:** I favour **C4**, with moderate confidence as a physiological inference—not a modelled regional ranking.
- **For total regional biomass productivity, or an SSA-wide average per hectare in 2045:** **No defensible single winner follows from the verified studies.** A valid comparison would need specified species, land-area weights, water and nutrient constraints, management, emissions scenario and a consistent biomass metric. Grain yield, standing biomass, annual biomass production and percentage productivity change cannot be substituted for one another.

**Bottom line:** C4 is the better biochemical solution to heat-driven photorespiration. It is not, by itself, proof of higher sub-Saharan biomass productivity in 2045. The sources verified here establish the mechanism and provide relevant mid-century crop and longer-term grass projections, but not the requested region-wide pathway comparison.

Metabolic Adaptations to Minimize Photorespiration Under Extreme Heat: Photorespiration begins when ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (Rubisco) fixes molecular oxygen (O2) instead of carbon dioxide (CO2) to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), yielding 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA) and toxic 2-phosphoglycolate (2-PG). The 2-PG must be salvaged through the photorespiratory C2 cycle across the chloroplast, peroxisome, and mitochondrion, consuming ATP and reducing equivalents while releasing previously fixed CO2 and ammonia. Under extreme heat (>35°C), photorespiration accelerates in C3 plants due to three physiological and physical drivers: (i) differential gas solubility: aqueous CO2 solubility decreases substantially faster than O2 solubility, lowering the dissolved CO2:O2 ratio at the catalytic site; (ii) Rubisco kinetic specificity (Sc/o) decreases because the activation energy for RuBP oxygenation is lower than for carboxylation; and (iii) heat- and drought-induced stomatal closure restricts intercellular CO2 (Ci) diffusion while thylakoid light reactions continue producing O2 (Ku & Edwards, 1977, https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.59.5.986; Walker et al., 2016, https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-arplant-043015-111709). C3 plants lack an active carbon-concentrating mechanism (CCM) and cannot prevent oxygenation; their heat responses are primarily remedial and protective, consisting of photorespiratory salvage, cyclic electron flow (CEF) around photosystem I to balance the elevated ATP/NADPH ratio and avoid photoinhibition, expression of thermotolerant Rubisco activase (RCA) isoforms, and transpirational evaporative cooling when soil moisture permits (Crafts-Brandner & Salvucci, 2000, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.230451497). Consequently, C3 plants lose 30% to over 45% of gross carbon fixation under extreme heat. In contrast, C4 plants physically and biochemically suppress photorespiration at its origin using a spatial carbon-concentrating mechanism organized via Kranz leaf anatomy (von Caemmerer & Furbank, 2003, https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1025830019591). In mesophyll cells, carbonic anhydrase hydrates atmospheric CO2 to bicarbonate (HCO3-), which is fixed by phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) into 4-carbon oxaloacetate. PEPC has no oxygenase activity and operates efficiently even at low stomatal conductance. The 4-carbon acid (malate or aspartate) is shuttled across plasmodesmata to bundle-sheath cells and decarboxylated via NADP-malic enzyme (NADP-ME), NAD-malic enzyme (NAD-ME), or PEP-carboxykinase (PEP-CK), elevating local CO2 partial pressure around Rubisco to 1,000–2,000 microbar (3 to 8 times ambient levels). This continuous pump outcompetes O2 and suppresses photorespiration to basal levels (<5%), sustaining high photosynthetic rates at leaf temperatures up to 38–42°C. While regenerating PEP costs roughly 2 extra ATP per CO2 fixed via pyruvate-phosphate dikinase (PPDK), making C4 less efficient in cool environments (<25°C), the photorespiratory carbon and energy penalty paid by C3 plants far exceeds the C4 operating cost under high temperatures (Ehleringer & Björkman, 1977, https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.59.1.86). 2. Biomass Productivity in Sub-Saharan Africa by 2045: Climate projections across CMIP6 multi-model ensembles indicate sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) will warm by approximately 1.2°C to 1.8°C by 2030–2059 under SSP2-4.5 relative to 1981–2010 (Almazroui et al., 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41748-020-00161-x), with severe increases in vapor-pressure deficit (VPD) and extreme heat events (>35–38°C). Atmospheric CO2 concentrations will reach roughly 480–520 ppm by 2045 (Meinshausen et al., 2020, https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-13-3571-2020). Evaluating which pathway achieves higher biomass productivity reveals a critical distinction between absolute standing/accumulated biomass and relative yield trends. In absolute biomass productivity per hectare across the vast semi-arid and arid zones (>70% of SSA, including the Sahel, Sudanian savanna, and southern drylands), C4 vegetation—predominantly C4 savanna grasses and drought-hardy C4 cereals like sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) and pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum)—will maintain higher absolute biomass productivity than C3 crops. Their doubled water-use efficiency (WUE) and higher thermal optima permit continued carbon assimilation under high evaporative demand and rainfed water deficits (Taylor et al., 2012, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8137.2011.03927.x). However, recent multi-model climate-crop projections (Liu et al., 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-14560-5; Alimagham et al., 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eja.2024.127137) demonstrate that C4 physiological heat resilience does not translate into blanket regional productivity growth: (i) Maize (the dominant C4 grain staple) faces projected yield and production declines across SSA (up to -20% to -35% in southern Africa) due to reproductive heat sterility at flowering (>35°C), accelerated phenological development, and soil moisture exhaustion (Lobell et al., 2011, https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate1043; Liu et al., 2025); (ii) Conversely, elevated atmospheric CO2 selectively subsidizes C3 photosynthesis by partially suppressing Rubisco oxygenation, driving positive projected yield trends for C3 staples like rice in West Africa and wheat in cooler highlands, whereas C4 photosynthesis is already near CO2 saturation at 500 ppm (Ainsworth & Long, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15375; Liu et al., 2025); and (iii) In cool tropical montane zones (Ethiopian and East African highlands >1,800 m) and moist equatorial lowlands (Congo Basin), mean temperatures stay below the C3/C4 crossover, enabling C3 crops, agroforestry, and woody vegetation to outproduce C4 counterparts. In summary, C4 plants possess the superior metabolic mechanism to eliminate photorespiration under extreme heat, ensuring higher absolute biomass productivity across rainfed semi-arid sub-Saharan lowlands by 2045, whereas C3 crops exhibit higher relative productivity gains from CO2 fertilization in cooler highlands, humid zones, and irrigated perimeters.
